title: Evolution Spell 1: Inheritance
lessonSummary: Great! Your child class inherits everything from its parent.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: a child class inherits a method.
Write the class Hero with `__init__(self, name)` and `introduce(self)` (prints I am Aria.) and the child class Warrior(Hero) with only `pass`. Create Warrior("Aria") and call `introduce()`.
tasks.codeTemplate: # 🎯 Your solution here:

tasks.instruction: The class Hero is given. Write Mage(Hero) with a **new** method `draw_weapon(self)` that prints Thorin draws the sword. (name from `self`). Create Mage("Thorin") and call `introduce()` first, then `draw_weapon()`.

validation.expected:
I am Thorin.
Thorin draws the sword.

tasks.instruction: The classes Hero, Warrior(Hero) and Mage(Hero) are given. Create Warrior("Aria") and check with `isinstance` whether it belongs to Hero and whether it belongs to Mage. Print both results on two lines.

title: Evolution Spell 2: Overriding Methods
lessonSummary: Nice! Children may do things differently from their parents.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: an overridden method.

validation.expected:
Aria fights bare-handed.
Thorin swings the sword.

The class Hero is given. Override `fight` in Mage(Hero) (prints casts a fireball. after the name). Call `fight()` for Hero("Luna") and for Mage("Thorin") – Luna first, then Thorin.

validation.expected:

Thorin casts a fireball.

title: Evolution Spell 3: super() and __init__
lessonSummary: Well done! You connect parent and child with super().

tasks.instruction: Run this example: a constructor with super().

The class Hero is given. Write Warrior(Hero) with `__init__(self, name, strength=30)` that sets the name via `super().__init__(name)` and stores `strength`. Create Warrior("Aria", 45) and print exactly Aria 45.
The class Hero is given. Write Mage(Hero) with `__init__(self, name, mana=50)` and `super()`. Create Mage("Thorin") without a second value and print exactly Thorin 50.

The classes Hero and Warrior (with an overridden `fight`) are given. Write Master(Warrior) that overrides `fight`: first `super().fight()`, then a second line Aria is a master!. Create Master("Aria") and call `fight()`.

validation.expected:
Aria swings the sword.
Aria is a master!

tasks.instruction: Run this example: the same method, three classes.

validation.expected:
Luna fights bare-handed.
Aria swings the sword.
Thorin casts a fireball.

tasks.instruction: The classes Hero, Warrior and Mage are given. Write a function `los(figure)` that calls `figure.fight()`. Call it for Warrior("Aria") and Mage("Thorin") one after the other.

validation.expected:
Aria swings the sword.
Thorin casts a fireball.

tasks.instruction: The classes are given, and so is the list `team = [Warrior("Aria"), Mage("Thorin"), Warrior("Luna"), Hero("Thorin")]`. Count with `isinstance` how many objects belong to Warrior and print exactly Count: 2.

The crowd cheers.

title: Extra Challenge 4: Everything Together
lessonSummary: Done: inheritance, dictionaries, randomness and JSON work together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – dictionary of classes: the classes are given. Build `klassen = {"Warrior": Warrior, "Mage": Mage}` and create an object through the name `klassen["Warrior"]("Aria")`. Call `fight()`.
Step 2 – randomness: the classes are given. Pick a class with `random.choice([Warrior, Mage])`, create an object from it and print `isinstance(object, Hero)` (True).

Step 3 – save as JSON: the classes are given. Create Warrior("Aria") and build `daten = {"typ": type(f).__name__, "name": f.name}` (`type(f).__name__` gives the class name as text). Print `json.dumps(daten)`.

Step 4 – load JSON: the classes and the text `text = '{"typ": "Warrior", "name": "Aria"}'` are given. Read it with `json.loads`, look up the class in the dictionary `klassen` and rebuild the object. Call `fight()`.
